title: Cap. 7 Rat. 11 close: Prosper/Hilary/Augustine/Fulgentius on special saving purpose
pass_a_gloss: That it is Pelagian to transfer the fruit of Christ’s death, that is, eternal life, from the special intention of God to a special operation of free choice, is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. It is plain also from Hilary’s Letter to the same Augustine, where the Remnants of the Pelagians think eternal life so proposed and set forth to all in Christ’s death that they utterly deny any singular or special purpose of God concerning saving the elect through this death of Christ, and recall this whole discrimination of those saved through Christ’s death and of the unsaved to human wills. And on the contrary, that the orthodox recognized a special and hidden purpose in God accepting the sacrifice of Christ’s death, and in Christ offering it, concerning its efficacious and fruitful application to certain persons, is no less clear from Augustine’s books On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and others written against the Pelagians and Semipelagians, in which this—concerning the special will of saving the elect through Christ—if not the only, is nevertheless the primary conclusion. The same can be said of Prosper and Fulgentius, who everywhere assert that the efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ is from the efficacious and special Divine will destinating Christ to the elect in a special manner, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to themselves as it may chance.
pass_b_english: That it is Pelagian to shift the fruit of Christ’s death—eternal life—from God’s special intention to a special act of free choice is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. Hilary’s Letter to Augustine shows the same: the Pelagian remnants treat eternal life in Christ’s death as so set before all that they flatly deny any singular purpose of God to save the elect by that death, and put the whole divide between the saved and the unsaved down to human wills. Against them, the orthodox saw a special hidden purpose in God accepting Christ’s death-sacrifice and in Christ offering it—toward efficacious fruitful application to certain persons. That is clear from Augustine’s On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and his other anti-Pelagian and anti-Semipelagian books, where the special will to save the elect through Christ is if not the only then the chief conclusion. Prosper and Fulgentius say the same throughout: efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ comes from God’s efficacious special will destinating Christ to the elect in a special way, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to itself as chance may have it.
source_text: Quod Pelagianum sit, fructum mortis Christi, id est, vitam aeternam, a speciali intentione Dei ad specialem operationem liberi arbitrii transferre, patet ex Prosperi Epistola ad Augustinum. Patet etiam ex Hilarii ad eundem Augustinum Epistola, ubi Reliquiae Pelagianorum in morte Christi vitam aeternam sic omnibus propositam & expositam opinantur, ut singulare aliquod sive speciale propositum Dei de salvandis electis per hanc mortem Christi prorsus pernegent, & totum hoc discrimen servatorum per mortem Christi & non-servatorum ad humanas voluntates revocent. Jam & contra, orthodoxos speciale & arcanum propositum agnovisse in Deo acceptante sacrificium mortis Christi, Christoque illud offerente, de applicatione ejusdem efficaci & fructuosa ad certas personas, non minus clarum est ex libris Augustini De Praedestinatione sanctorum, De Bono perseverantiae, aliisque contra Pelagianos & Semipelagianos conscriptis, in quibus haec, de speciali voluntate salvandi electos per Christum, si non unica, primaria tamen conclusio est. De Prospero & Fulgentio idem dici potest, qui passim asserunt efficacem salutis consecutionem in Christo ab efficaci & speciali voluntate Divina Christum electis speciali modo destinante, non a libero hominum arbitrio Christi mortem ac merita sibi, prout contigerit, applicante.
